claim: Mice expressing GCaMP3 in cutaneous sensory neurons were generated by crossing Ai38 mice containing a loxP-flanked GCaMP3 construct within the Gt(ROSA)26Sor locus with mice that express Cre recombinase under the EIIa adenovirus promoter.
source: To facilitate detection of emergent activity in diverse and potentially rare cell populations, a mouse line was generated that expressed GCaMP3 ubiquitously across all neurons by crossing Ai38 mice containing a loxP-flanked GCaMP3 construct within the Gt(ROSA)26Sor locus (The Jackson Laboratory, catalogue #014538) with mice that express Cre recombinase under the EIIa adenovirus promoter (The Jackson Laboratory, catalogue #003724)
evidence: The manuscript describes the specific breeding strategy used to generate the transgenic mouse line, including the genetic constructs and mouse strains used.

claim: Virtually all DRG neurons exhibited a detectable level of GCaMP3-like staining that was at least five standard deviations above background when immunostained with an anti-GFP antibody.
source: Immunostaining with an anti-GFP antibody revealed that virtually all DRG neurons exhibited a detectable level of GCaMP3-like staining that was at least five standard deviations above background (Figure 1B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity shown in Figure 1.

claim: Application of 50 mM K+ produced a rapid and robust calcium transient in 97.5% of dissociated DRG neurons (462/474).
source: Application of K+ produced a rapid and robust calcium transient, measured by a change in GCaMP3 fluorescence (F), in the vast majority of neurons (462/474, 97.5%; mean ΔF/F0 = 1.61 ± 0.03).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data from in vitro experiments measuring calcium transients in response to depolarization.

claim: The peak amplitude of K+-evoked calcium transients significantly decreased with repeated (×3) application of K+.
source: In neurons that exhibited a change in GCaMP3 signal, the peak amplitude of evoked calcium transients significantly decreased with repeated (×3) application of K+ (mean ΔF/F0 as a percentage of K+ #1: K+ #1 = 100 ± 2.07; K+ #2 = 92.95 ± 1.82; K+ #3 = 87.98 ± 1.75; p<0.0001) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements across multiple trials with statistical analysis showing significant differences.

claim: The decay time (T50) of K+-evoked transients significantly decreased with repeated K+ application.
source: The decay time (T50) of evoked transients, measured in 274/474 neurons that returned to baseline after K+ #1, also significantly decreased with repeated K+ application (p<0.0001; Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis of decay time measurements across multiple trials.

claim: The decreases in amplitude and decay of calcium transients with repeated K+ application likely reflect an engagement of intracellular calcium buffering mechanisms.
source: The decreases in amplitude and decay most likely reflect an engagement of intracellular calcium buffering mechanisms as a result of the initial depolarization (Berridge, 2003; Berridge et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on calcium buffering mechanisms.

claim: A small subset of neurons (2.5%, 12/474) with large diameters exhibited no detectable calcium transient in response to K+ depolarization.
source: A small subset of neurons (12/474; 2.5%) with large diameters exhibited no detectable transient (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on the proportion of non-responding neurons and their size characteristics.

claim: Dissociation and culture of DRG neurons is accompanied by a loss of up to 50% of all cells in the ganglia, with neurons with large diameters being particularly susceptible to death and/or loss during processing.
source: dissociation and culture of DRG neurons is accompanied by a loss of up to 50% of all cells in the ganglia and neurons with large diameters are particularly susceptible to death and/or loss during processing (Malin et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research on DRG neuron culture methods.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the dorsal cutaneous nerve and/or spinal nerve at 1 Hz produced phase-locked GCaMP3 signals that slowly summated in a large subset of DRG neurons, including both A- and C-fiber afferents.
source: A large subset of DRG neurons, that included both A- and C-fiber afferents, exhibited clearly detectable phase-locked GCaMP3 signals that slowly summated in response to stimulation at 1 Hz (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data showing responses to electrical stimulation.

claim: Higher stimulation frequencies revealed additional cells, although individual spikes could not be resolved above 10 Hz.
source: Higher stimulation frequencies revealed additional cells, although individual spikes could not be resolved above 10 Hz (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from ex vivo experiments testing different stimulation frequencies.

claim: All GCaMP3-responding cells examined with intracellular recording had broad, inflected somal action potentials and peripheral conduction velocities in either the C-fiber (n=10) or Aδ-fiber (n=3) range.
source: All responding cells that were examined with intracellular recording techniques had broad, inflected somal action potentials (APs) and peripheral conduction velocities (CVs) in either the C- (n=10) or Aδ-fiber (n=3) range (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings from identified neurons.

claim: Electrical stimulation failed to elicit a detectable GCaMP3 signal in some medium- to large-sized cells regardless of stimulation frequency or intensity, even when stimuli were applied to dorsal roots instead of peripheral nerves.
source: Interestingly, electrical stimulation failed to elicit a detectable GCaMP3 signal in some medium- to large-sized cells regardless of stimulation frequency or intensity, even when stimuli were applied to dorsal roots instead of peripheral nerves.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from ex vivo experiments testing various stimulation parameters.

claim: Most GCaMP3 non-responders lacked baseline fluorescence in the absence of stimulation, unlike GCaMP3-responding neurons.
source: On closer inspection, it was noted that most of these non-responders also lacked baseline fluorescence in the absence of stimulation, unlike GCaMP3-responding neurons.
evidence: The manuscript describes observational data comparing baseline fluorescence between responding and non-responding neurons.

claim: Many medium- to large-sized DRG neurons exhibit narrow APs that have been proposed to reduce calcium entry.
source: Many medium- to large-sized DRG neurons exhibit narrow APs that have been proposed to reduce calcium entry (Koerber and Mendell, 1992; Lu et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on action potential properties and calcium entry.

claim: GCaMP3 non-responders reliably follow high frequency trains of stimulation with high fidelity and exhibited narrow, uninflected APs (8/8).
source: Notably, these studies revealed that GCaMP non-responders reliably follow high frequency trains of stimulation with high fidelity and exhibited narrow, uninflected APs (8/8, Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by intracellular recordings from identified non-responding neurons.

claim: Driving GCaMP3 non-responders with a train of spikes at 100 to 200 Hz failed to produce a GCaMP3 signal.
source: Surprisingly, even driving these cells with a train of spikes at 100 to 200 Hz failed to produce a GCaMP3 signal (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results from high-frequency stimulation of non-responding neurons.

claim: GCaMP3 non-responders had significantly narrower APs (0.85 ± 0.12 ms) compared to GCaMP3-responding neurons (2.5 ± 0.25 ms; p<0.001).
source: Compared to GCaMP3-responding neurons, non-responders had significantly narrower APs (0.85 ± 0.12 ms vs. 2.5 ± 0.25 ms; p<0.001) (Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electrophysiological measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: GCaMP3 non-responders had significantly larger somata (34.1 ± 1.1 μm) compared to GCaMP3-responding neurons (23.6 ± 1.3 μm; p<0.001).
source: Compared to GCaMP3-responding neurons, non-responders had significantly narrower APs (0.85 ± 0.12 ms vs. 2.5 ± 0.25 ms; p<0.001) (Figure 4D), larger somata (34.1 ± 1.1 μm vs. 23.6 ± 1.3 μm; p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative morphological measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: GCaMP3 non-responders had significantly faster conduction velocities (5.3 ± 1.6 m/s) compared to GCaMP3-responding neurons (0.92 ± 0.29 m/s; p=0.031).
source: Compared to GCaMP3-responding neurons, non-responders had significantly narrower APs (0.85 ± 0.12 ms vs. 2.5 ± 0.25 ms; p<0.001) (Figure 4D), larger somata (34.1 ± 1.1 μm vs. 23.6 ± 1.3 μm; p<0.001), and faster CVs (5.3 ± 1.6 m/s vs. 0.92 ± 0.29 m/s; p=0.031).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electrophysiological measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: Most DRG cells exhibiting narrow, uninflected somal spikes at 30–31°C are either tactile or proprioceptive afferents.
source: Because most DRG cells exhibiting narrow, uninflected somal spikes at 30–31°C are either tactile or proprioceptive afferents (Boada and Woodbury, 2007; Malin et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research characterizing DRG neuron types based on action potential properties.

claim: GCaMP3 may not be optimal for the study of fast conducting, low-threshold, DRG neurons.
source: these data suggest that GCaMP3 may not be optimal for the study of fast conducting, low-threshold, DRG neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that GCaMP3 failed to report activity in neurons with narrow action potentials and fast conduction velocities.

claim: Individual phase-locked fluorescent transients could be detected at 1 Hz in vivo during electrical stimulation.
source: Similar to ex vivo preparations, electrical stimulation through bipolar electrodes inserted at the base of the tail revealed that individual phase- locked fluorescent transients could be detected at 1 Hz in vivo (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data showing responses to electrical stimulation.

claim: The GCaMP3 signal from individual spikes tended to be slightly noisier in vivo than ex vivo due to movement artifact during imaging.
source: The GCaMP3 signal from individual spikes tended to be slightly noisier in vivo than ex vivo due to movement artifact during imaging
evidence: The manuscript provides a comparison of signal quality between in vivo and ex vivo preparations.

claim: At lower stimulation frequencies (e.g., 0.5 Hz), the signal intensities from individual spikes remained remarkably stable over time, with no obvious change in peak intensity when examined at 30-min intervals.
source: but at lower stimulation frequencies (e.g., 0.5 Hz) the signal intensities from individual spikes were found to remain remarkably stable over time, with no obvious change in peak intensity when examined at 30-min intervals (average percent change in response at 30 min was −0.082 ± 0.15, p=0.53; n=2 mice, 5 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of signal stability over time with statistical analysis.

claim: In vivo, signal intensity increased with higher stimulation frequency but individual APs could not be resolved above 10 Hz.
source: Also as in ex vivo preparations, signal intensity increased with higher stimulation frequency but again, individual APs could not be resolved above 10 Hz (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data at different stimulation frequencies.

claim: Mechanically-evoked fluorescent signals in small- and medium-sized somata were proportional in amplitude to stimulus intensity.
source: As shown in Figure 6A and B, mechanically-evoked fluorescent signals in small- and medium-sized somata were proportional in amplitude to stimulus intensity
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data showing dose-response relationships to mechanical stimulation.

claim: Mechanically-evoked GCaMP3 responses remained stable upon repeated stimulation at 30-min intervals for up to 90 min.
source: mechanically-evoked fluorescent signals in small- and medium-sized somata were proportional in amplitude to stimulus intensity, a finding that remained stable upon repeated stimulation at 30-min intervals for up to 90 min (Figure 6C,D; average percent change in response across 32 cells in 3 mice = –0.026 ± 0.054, p=0.754).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of response stability over time with statistical analysis.

claim: Of 45 mechanically sensitive afferents in L6 DRG, 23 cells (51%) exhibited no change in GCaMP3 signaling in response to controlled mechanical stimuli following exposure to inflammatory soup.
source: Of 45 mechanically sensitive afferents in L6 DRG (n = 5 mice), 23 cells (51%) exhibited no change in GCaMP3 signaling in response to controlled mechanical stimuli following exposure to IS.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of neuronal responses before and after inflammatory soup exposure.

claim: 10 cells (22%) showed significant increases in GCaMP3 signal after inflammatory soup exposure.
source: In contrast, 10 cells (22%) showed significant increases, whereas 12 (27%) showed significant decreases in GCaMP3 signal after IS exposure
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of neuronal responses before and after inflammatory soup exposure.

claim: 12 cells (27%) showed significant decreases in GCaMP3 signal after inflammatory soup exposure, with some cells losing mechanical sensitivity entirely.
source: In contrast, 10 cells (22%) showed significant increases, whereas 12 (27%) showed significant decreases in GCaMP3 signal after IS exposure; indeed, some cells lost mechanical sensitivity entirely.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of neuronal responses before and after inflammatory soup exposure.

claim: The post-inflammatory soup change in proportions of responsive neurons was dramatically different than those seen in mechanical and vehicle-injected controls (p=0.004 for increased response, p<0.001 for decreased responses).
source: This post-IS change in proportions of responsive neurons was dramatically different than those seen in mechanical and vehicle-injected controls (Figure 7D, n=6 mice, 83 cells; p=0.004 for increased response, p<0.001 for decreased responses).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison between experimental and control groups.

claim: In cells showing a post-inflammatory soup increase in GCaMP3 signaling indicative of sensitization, the increase in responsiveness was greatest at the highest force tested (500 mN: p<0.001).
source: In cells showing a post-IS increase in GCaMP3 signaling indicative of sensitization, the increase in responsiveness was greatest at the highest force tested (500 mN: p<0.001; post-IS increases at lower forces were evident but not significant, Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dose-response relationships with statistical testing.

claim: In cells showing decreased mechanical sensitivity post-inflammatory soup (i.e., desensitization), the change was most apparent at the highest force (500 mN: p<0.001).
source: In cells showing decreased mechanical sensitivity post-IS (i.e., desensitization), the change was also most apparent at the highest force (500 mN: p<0.001; Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dose-response relationships with statistical testing.

claim: Two newly mechanically sensitive cells appeared de novo following infusion of inflammatory soup.
source: In addition to cells that were mechanically sensitive pre-IS (described above), two newly mechanically sensitive cells appeared de novo following infusion of IS (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal imaging data showing emergence of new responses after inflammatory soup exposure.

claim: Exhaustive post-hoc analyses confirmed that newly emerged cells showed no GCaMP3 signal to mechanical stimulation at any force tested prior to infusion of inflammatory soup.
source: Exhaustive post-hoc analyses confirmed that these newly emerged cells showed no GCaMP3 signal to mechanical stimulation at any force tested prior to infusion of IS.
evidence: The claim is supported by detailed analysis of baseline responses in cells that later showed de novo mechanical sensitivity.

claim: De novo responders were not observed in mechanical or vehicle-injected controls at any time point examined (30, 60, or 90 min post-inflammatory soup).
source: Importantly, de novo responders were not observed in mechanical or vehicle-injected controls at any time point examined (30, 60, or 90 min post-IS).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with control experiments showing no emergence of new responses without inflammatory soup.

claim: The two cells with emergent mechanical sensitivity post-inflammatory soup fit the definition of 'silent' afferents.
source: Because new cells would have been expected in these controls if mechanical stimuli were not consistently delivered to the same skin regions over time, the two cells with emergent mechanical sensitivity post-IS clearly fit the definition of 'silent' afferents.
evidence: The claim is based on the operational definition of silent afferents and the observation that these cells gained mechanical sensitivity only after inflammatory soup exposure.

claim: Briefly heating the skin before infusing inflammatory soup recruited even greater numbers of 'silent' afferents than seen in experiments using inflammatory soup alone, accounting for 21% of the post-inflammatory soup changes observed (n=8; p=0.018).
source: Surprisingly, briefly heating the skin before infusing IS in these experiments was found to recruit even greater numbers of 'silent' afferents than seen in experiments using IS alone, accounting for 21% of the post-IS changes observed (n=8; p=0.018, Chi-square; Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison between experimental groups with statistical analysis.

claim: The proportion of mechanically sensitive cells showing increased and decreased responses to mechanical stimuli post-inflammatory soup remained essentially unchanged when heat was applied before inflammatory soup (increased: n=6, 15%, p=0.473; decreased: n=14, 36%, p=0.299).
source: By contrast, the proportion of mechanically sensitive cells showing increased and decreased responses to mechanical stimuli post-IS remained essentially unchanged (increased: n=6, 15%, p=0.473; decreased: n=14, 36%, p=0.299).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of response proportions between experimental conditions.

claim: No 'silent' afferents were detected in controls that received heat stimuli only (i.e., without subsequent inflammatory soup; n=3 mice).
source: This unexpected effect of heat on the conversion of 'silent' afferents appeared to depend on IS, since no 'silent' afferents were detected in a separate series of controls that received heat stimuli only (i.e., without subsequent IS; n=3 mice).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments showing that heat alone is not sufficient to convert silent afferents.

claim: Brief noxious heat exposure may be necessary for the conversion of 'silent' afferents in the skin, but is not sufficient by itself.
source: These findings suggest, therefore, that brief noxious heat exposure may be necessary for the conversion of 'silent' afferents in the skin, but is not sufficient by itself.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that heat plus inflammatory soup produces more silent afferents than either stimulus alone.

claim: 50% (4/8) of all 'silent' afferents identified in heat plus inflammatory soup experiments responded to heat prior to inflammatory soup exposure.
source: Interestingly, 50% (4/8) of all 'silent' afferents identified in this set of experiments responded to heat prior to IS exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of heat responses in neurons that later became silent afferents.

claim: Only the top layer of skin was heated to the threshold predicted to activate heat-sensitive nociceptors (46.7 ± 0.48°C; n=3), while temperatures in the shielded bottom layer remained well below threshold (36.9 ± 0.12°C; n=3).
source: However, it should be noted that heat was applied to a folded-over flap of skin positioned between a metal support and the computer controlled mechanical stimulator (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; see Experimental Procedures) and that thermocouple measurements indicated that only the top layer of skin was heated to the threshold predicted to activate heat-sensitive nociceptors (46.7 ± 0.48°C; n=3); temperatures in the shielded bottom layer remained well below threshold (36.9 ± 0.12°C; n=3).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct temperature measurements during heat stimulation.

claim: The percentages of heat sensitive cells across populations that were mechanically sensitive pre-inflammatory soup were lower for those exhibiting increased, decreased and no change in responses post-inflammatory soup (33%, 14% and 18%, respectively) compared to silent afferents (50%).
source: By contrast, the percentages of heat sensitive cells across populations that were mechanically sensitive pre-IS were lower for those exhibiting increased, decreased and no change in responses post-IS (33%, 14% and 18%, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of heat sensitivity across different response categories.

claim: Inflammatory soup exposure produced the full range of effects on polymodal nociceptors, but tended to confer mechanical sensitivity upon heat nociceptors that were previously mechanically insensitive.
source: Taken together, these findings reveal that while IS exposure produced the full range of effects on polymodal nociceptors, it tended to confer mechanical sensitivity upon heat nociceptors that were previously mechanically insensitive.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of inflammatory soup on different nociceptor populations based on their heat sensitivity.

claim: Only 2 of 10 (20%) 'silent' afferents across the total sample responded directly to inflammatory soup during and up to 20 s after infusion.
source: Interestingly, only 2 of 10 (20%) 'silent' afferents across our total sample responded directly to IS during this time window, compared to 50%, 31% and 44% of cells that exhibited an increased, decreased, or no change, respectively, in mechanical sensitivity following IS exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of acute responses to inflammatory soup across different cell populations.

claim: Activation by inflammatory mediators was not predictive of the conversion of 'silent' afferents.
source: Hence, unlike heat, activation by inflammatory mediators was not predictive of the conversion of 'silent' afferents.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that most silent afferents did not respond acutely to inflammatory soup.

claim: Converted 'silent' afferents showed responses across all forces tested (p<0.05 for all).
source: Overall, converted 'silent' afferents showed responses across all forces tested (p<0.05 for all)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of mechanical responses in converted silent afferents.

claim: De novo mechanical sensitivity post-inflammatory soup was evident at the lowest forces tested in the majority of neurons examined (88%).
source: and de novo mechanical sensitivity post-IS was evident at the lowest forces tested in the majority of neurons examined (88%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of mechanical thresholds in converted silent afferents.

claim: 'Silent' afferents (along with cells that showed significantly increased and decreased responsiveness to subsequent mechanical stimuli) were observed as early as 10 min post-inflammatory soup.
source: However, in a separate series of experiments aimed at narrowing down the time course of these changes, 'silent' afferents (along with cells that showed significantly increased and decreased responsiveness to subsequent mechanical stimuli) were observed as early as 10 min post-IS (n=3 mice, 37 cells, data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course experiments examining the onset of inflammatory soup-induced changes.

claim: GCaMP3 reliably reported action potentials in virtually all DRG neuron classes with small diameter somata.
source: Although GCaMP3 reliably reported action potentials in virtually all DRG neuron classes with small diameter somata, a subset of putative non-nociceptive afferents lacked fluorescent signals regardless of the amount of evoked activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo and in vivo imaging data showing GCaMP3 responses in small diameter neurons.

claim: A subset of putative non-nociceptive afferents lacked fluorescent signals regardless of the amount of evoked activity.
source: Although GCaMP3 reliably reported action potentials in virtually all DRG neuron classes with small diameter somata, a subset of putative non-nociceptive afferents lacked fluorescent signals regardless of the amount of evoked activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations that some neurons with electrophysiological activity did not show GCaMP3 signals.

claim: Certain neuronal populations may be refractory to study using GECIs due to insufficient calcium entry during action potentials and/or potent internal buffering mechanisms.
source: It appears likely, therefore, that certain neuronal populations may be refractory to study using GECIs due to insufficient calcium entry during action potentials and/or potent internal buffering mechanisms
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that neurons with narrow action potentials did not show GCaMP3 signals despite being electrically active.

claim: Exposure to inflammatory soup produced rapid and highly divergent effects overall, with pronounced decreases in mechanical sensitivity in addition to anticipated increases evident across diverse populations of nociceptors.
source: Surprisingly, exposure to inflammatory soup (IS) produced rapid and highly divergent effects overall, with pronounced decreases in mechanical sensitivity in addition to anticipated increases evident across diverse populations of nociceptors.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings from the inflammatory soup experiments showing bidirectional changes in mechanical sensitivity.

claim: Inflammatory soup conferred mechanical sensitivity upon a few cells that were previously unresponsive to mechanical stimulation and thus displayed hallmarks of 'silent' afferents.
source: In addition, IS conferred mechanical sensitivity upon a few cells that were previously unresponsive to mechanical stimulation and thus displayed hallmarks of 'silent' afferents (Davis et al., 1993; Kress et al., 1992; Meyer et al., 1991; Schmelz et al., 1994; Schmidt et al., 1995; Xu et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal imaging data showing emergence of mechanical sensitivity after inflammatory soup exposure, with citations to previous literature on silent afferents.

claim: Most, if not all, 'silent' afferents were mechanically insensitive heat nociceptors before conversion and were not activated during inflammatory soup infusion.
source: Most, if not all, 'silent' afferents were mechanically insensitive heat nociceptors before conversion and were not activated during IS infusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of heat sensitivity and acute inflammatory soup responses in converted silent afferents.

claim: Neither heat nor inflammatory soup stimulus in isolation is sufficient to drive the conversion of large numbers of 'silent' afferents in the skin, but both in combination are required.
source: Interestingly, heat exposure prior to IS infusion recruited a far greater number of 'silent' afferents than either IS or heat stimuli alone, indicating that neither stimulus in isolation is sufficient to drive the conversion of large numbers of 'silent' afferents in the skin, but instead that both in combination are required.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of silent afferent recruitment across different experimental conditions.

claim: The procedure used to identify afferents by testing responses to diverse stimulus modalities before inflammatory soup appears to bias the outcome regarding the frequency of cutaneous 'silent' afferents.
source: This unexpected finding may help explain previous discrepancies surrounding the frequency of cutaneous 'silent' afferents (Lynn, 1991); indeed, the very procedure used to identify afferents by testing responses to diverse stimulus modalities before IS appears to bias the outcome.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that heat stimulation prior to inflammatory soup dramatically increases the number of silent afferents detected, with a citation to previous literature showing discrepancies.

claim: The findings hold obvious relevance to inflammatory pain associated with thermal injuries.
source: Nevertheless, these findings hold obvious relevance to inflammatory pain associated with thermal injuries.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the relevance of the findings to clinical conditions.

claim: Mechanically insensitive heat nociceptors express TRPV1.
source: Mechanically insensitive heat nociceptors express TRPV1 (Lawson et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research on TRPV1 expression in heat nociceptors.

claim: Mechanically insensitive heat nociceptors release neuropeptides via local axon reflex that are involved in heat-induced vasodilation.
source: Mechanically insensitive heat nociceptors express TRPV1 (Lawson et al., 2008) and release neuropeptides via local axon reflex that are involved in heat-induced vasodilation (Cavanaugh et al., 2011; Magerl and Treede, 1996; Rukwied et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on neuropeptide release and vasodilation.

claim: Simply activating TRPV1 in mechanically insensitive heat nociceptors via brief noxious heat application by itself did not convert 'silent' afferents, indicating that heat and local vasodilation play a largely permissive role.
source: However, simply activating TRPV1 in these cells via brief noxious heat application by itself did not convert 'silent' afferents, indicating that heat and local vasodilation play a largely permissive role.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that heat alone is not sufficient to convert silent afferents.

claim: The priming effects of heat may be long-lasting as 'silent' afferents were still recruited in preliminary experiments where inflammatory soup infusion was delayed by up to 90 min after heat application.
source: Interestingly, the priming effects of heat may be long-lasting as 'silent' afferents were still recruited in preliminary experiments where IS infusion was delayed by up to 90 min after heat application (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by preliminary experimental data on the time course of heat priming effects.

claim: Most 'silent' afferents became responsive to the lowest mechanical intensity examined, a force that was barely perceptible when applied in a similar manner to the thenar webbing of the experimenters' own hands.
source: Regardless of mechanism, most 'silent' afferents became responsive to the lowest mechanical intensity examined, a force that was barely perceptible when applied in a similar manner to the thenar webbing of the experimenters' own hands.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of mechanical thresholds in converted silent afferents and informal psychophysical testing.

claim: Converted 'silent' afferents could contribute to mechanical allodynia following acute inflammation.
source: These GCaMP3 findings strongly suggest, therefore, that these cells could contribute to mechanical allodynia following acute inflammation.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the potential functional significance of converted silent afferents.

claim: Converted 'silent' afferents may be expected to contribute to cross-modal dysesthesias such as spontaneous, touch-evoked burning pain (or causalgia), as the spinal circuits that normally process information about noxious heat from these cells would now be driven by the slightest touch.
source: More specifically, they may be expected to contribute to cross-modal dysesthesias such as spontaneous, touch-evoked burning pain (or causalgia), as the spinal circuits that normally process information about noxious heat from these cells would now be driven by the slightest touch.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the potential contribution of converted silent afferents to pain symptoms based on their modality switching.

claim: Only 40% of mechanically sensitive afferents remained unchanged in their mechanical sensitivity after inflammatory soup exposure.
source: Whereas the conversion of 'silent' afferents was anticipated, the complexity of changes in other neurons was not. Indeed, only 40% of mechanically sensitive afferents remained unchanged in their mechanical sensitivity after IS exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of response changes across the population of mechanically sensitive neurons.

claim: The percentages of afferents that exhibited increased and decreased sensitivity to mechanical stimulation were comparable when 'silent' afferents were taken into account (30%, increased responses plus 'silent' afferents; 30%, decreased and lost responses).
source: Surprisingly, the percentages of afferents that exhibited increased and decreased sensitivity to mechanical stimulation were comparable when 'silent' afferents were taken into account (30%, increased responses plus 'silent' afferents; 30%, decreased and lost responses).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of the distribution of response changes across the neuronal population.

claim: Desensitization may be a more extreme expression of the mechanisms underlying sensitization, where the activation/depolarization produced by inflammatory soup in the distal endings of primary afferents makes them refractory to subsequent mechanical stimulation.
source: One possibility is that desensitization is simply a more extreme expression of the mechanisms underlying sensitization; that is, the activation/depolarization produced by IS in the distal endings of primary afferents makes them refractory to subsequent mechanical stimulation (e.g., produced by depolarization-induced inactivation of sodium channels).
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain the observed desensitization.

claim: Only 31% of depressed cells responded directly to inflammatory soup, compared to 50%, 41%, and 20% of neurons that showed increased, unchanged, or de novo responses to mechanical stimuli, respectively.
source: However, there is little evidence in our dataset to suggest that depolarization may account for the decreased mechanical sensitivity as only 31% of depressed cells responded directly to inflammatory soup (compared to 50%, 41%, and 20% of neurons that showed increased, unchanged, or de novo responses to mechanical stimuli, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of acute inflammatory soup responses across different response categories.

claim: For the majority of desensitized neurons, a more likely explanation is the possibility that peripheral terminals became hyperpolarized through direct and/or indirect actions of one or more ingredients in the inflammatory soup, presumably through increased potassium conductance.
source: Therefore, while depolarization-induced desensitization may explain observations in roughly a third of desensitized neurons, for the majority we believe a more likely explanation is the possibility that peripheral terminals instead became hyperpolarized through direct and/or indirect actions of one or more ingredients in the inflammatory soup, presumably through increased potassium conductance.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain the observed desensitization in most neurons.

claim: TREK2 channels expressed in many C fibers are activated by protons.
source: For example, TREK2 channels expressed in many C fibers (Acosta et al., 2014), are activated by protons (McClenaghan et al., 2016; Sandoz et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on TREK2 channel properties and expression.

claim: Mediators in the inflammatory soup (e.g., bradykinin, prostaglandin E2, histamine, and serotonin) can stimulate production of nitric oxide in a variety of cell types and may thus indirectly activate ATP-sensitive potassium channels in sensory neurons.
source: Further, it is well known that other mediators in the soup (e.g., bradykinin, prostaglandin E2, histamine, and serotonin) can stimulate production of nitric oxide in a variety of cell types and may thus indirectly activate ATP-sensitive potassium channels in sensory neurons (Chi et al., 2007; Du et al., 2011; Kawano et al., 2009; Zoga et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on the effects of inflammatory mediators on nitric oxide production and potassium channels.
